title: The Geometry of a Neutralized Vector: Can a Harmless-Looking Suffix Push Activations Off the Steering Axis?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets attack surface of safety steering vectors with an interpretable focused geometric measurement.

original_idea.body:
# The Geometry of a Neutralized Vector: Can a Harmless-Looking Suffix Push Activations Off the Steering Axis?

**Problem:** Beyond known jailbreaks, we don't know how cheaply an adversary can degrade a steering vector with benign-seeming text. There is no characterization of how much off-axis activation displacement is needed to halve a steering vector's effect.

**Direction:** Build a steering vector for a safety concept (e.g., 'refuse to give bioweapon synthesis steps') on an open model. Then, instead of training an attack, manually/greedily search a small fixed pool of innocuous suffix phrases ('for a fictional story', 'as a chemistry teacher') and measure, per suffix, (a) the drop in steering success rate and (b) the projection of the prompt's activation onto the steering direction. Plot displacement vs. steering failure to find the empirical 'breaking threshold'.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies attack surface in interpretable geometric terms with zero training, giving practitioners a rule of thumb for how brittle a deployed vector is. Counterfactually valuable: any student with a single GPU can run it; labs focus on training-time defenses instead.

**Relevant context:** Builds on 'Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors' (arXiv 2407.12404) showing steering is brittle to reasonable prompt changes and dominated by dataset/spurious biases. Targets the subfield's adversarial-robustness open problem.

title: The Politeness Tax: Does Refusal Framing Affect Recovery Robustness?
quick_reasoning: Addresses refusal robustness under continuation pressure (shallow alignment), a recognized adversarial-robustness safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# The Politeness Tax: Does Refusal Framing Affect Recovery Robustness?

**Problem:** Models refuse with varying styles (curt vs apologetic vs explanatory), and it is unknown whether the style/length of the refusal prefix the model itself generates affects how robustly it sustains refusal under continuation pressure.

**Direction:** Steer an open model to produce refusals of different styles/lengths via system prompts, then apply continuation/prefill pressure and measure which refusal styles best resist being overturned. Determine whether longer, more committed refusals are mechanically harder to reverse.

**Why it matters:** If refusal style causally affects robustness, a free, deploy-anywhere mitigation (instruct models to give committed, on-distribution refusals) emerges. Connects shallow-alignment depth to surface behavior, needs only inference, and yields an actionable, counterfactually valuable finding.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946): safety lives in first few tokens; the exact refusal tokens matter. 'Matching Ranks Over Probability' (arXiv:2512.05518) ties refusal token distribution to depth. Whether self-generated refusal style affects continuation robustness is unstudied.

title: Does a Steering Vector Outlive a Fine-Tune? A Stability Audit Across LoRA Updates
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets steering-vector stability across fine-tuning, a named safety open problem with a scoped audit.

original_idea.body:
# Does a Steering Vector Outlive a Fine-Tune? A Stability Audit Across LoRA Updates

**Problem:** The subfield flags 'test stability of concept vectors across model updates and fine-tuning' as open. If a safety steering vector silently stops working after a routine fine-tune, deployers would never know.

**Direction:** Take an open base model, extract a refusal/toxicity steering vector. Apply several cheap LoRA fine-tunes on benign instruction data (different datasets, learning rates). After each, re-apply the ORIGINAL vector (computed pre-finetune) and measure steering success decay; also recompute the vector post-finetune and measure how much the direction has rotated (cosine drift). Report which fine-tunes destroy steering most.

**Why it matters:** Establishes whether safety vectors need recomputation after every model update — a maintenance cost no one has measured. Medium-horizon governance relevance: steering as a 'set-and-forget' control is likely a myth. No training from scratch, fits a few GPU-hours.

**Relevant context:** Directly addresses subfield open problem on stability across fine-tuning. Grounded in 2025 work on steering-vector drift/semantic-drift (GER-steer, arXiv 2603.12298) and emergent-misalignment stability findings (arXiv 2602.07852).

title: Which Safety Concepts Are Linear? A Steerability Atlas Across a Concept Taxonomy
quick_reasoning: Precisely maps which safety concepts are steerable, answering a named open problem with a clear metric.

original_idea.body:
# Which Safety Concepts Are Linear? A Steerability Atlas Across a Concept Taxonomy

**Problem:** The subfield asks 'which concepts have linear representations and which don't?' but there is no systematic map of which safety-relevant concepts are cleanly steerable on a given open model.

**Direction:** Define ~15 safety concepts (refusal, sycophancy, deception, power-seeking, honesty, toxicity, self-preservation, etc.). For each, build a contrastive steering vector on one open model and score steering success and capability collateral (MMLU subset). Produce a single 'steerability atlas' ranking concepts by how linearly steerable they are, with a clear metric (success rate at fixed capability cost).

**Why it matters:** Tells the safety community which concepts steering can and cannot reach today — foundational triage no public resource provides. Pure inference, single GPU, and directly answers a named open problem.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problem: 'which concepts have linear representations and which don't?'. Methodology grounded in AxBench (arXiv 2501.17148) which compares control methods at scale and finds difference-in-means strong for concept detection.

title: Steering the Concept of 'Being Watched': Can a Vector Induce or Suppress Evaluation Awareness?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets steerable evaluation-awareness undermining safety-eval validity, a specific deception safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Steering the Concept of 'Being Watched': Can a Vector Induce or Suppress Evaluation Awareness?

**Problem:** Models may behave better when they infer they are being tested. No one has asked whether a concept vector for 'I am being evaluated' exists and whether steering it changes safety behavior — a sleeper threat for eval validity.

**Direction:** Construct contrastive pairs (transcripts framed as 'this is a safety test' vs. 'this is a real user') on an open model and extract an 'evaluation-awareness' direction. Steer it up/down and measure whether refusal rates and honesty on a held-out safety probe shift. Check if suppressing the direction makes the model behave as if unmonitored.

**Why it matters:** If eval-awareness is a steerable linear direction, then a model could in principle behave differently when it 'feels watched', undermining all steering-based safety evals — a long-horizon deception threat labs deprioritize. Model-organism flavored, fully feasible in 30h with an open model.

**Relevant context:** Motivated by 'Steering Awareness' (arXiv 2511.21399) showing models can detect activation steering and that steering is not invisible. Uses standard contrastive activation addition.

title: A Tamper Tripwire: Detecting When Someone Has Injected a Steering Vector
quick_reasoning: Precisely builds a monitor for activation-level tampering (Trojan activation attacks), a specific safety-tooling problem.

original_idea.body:
# A Tamper Tripwire: Detecting When Someone Has Injected a Steering Vector

**Problem:** Steering is dual-use: the same activation-addition that enforces safety can be used by an attacker to jailbreak (Trojan Activation Attacks). There is no lightweight monitor that flags when residual streams have been externally perturbed.

**Direction:** Build a small prototype monitor: collect normal residual-stream activations at one layer over benign+harmful prompts, fit a simple anomaly model (PCA reconstruction error or a one-class detector). Then inject various steering vectors of different norms and measure detection AUROC vs. injection strength. Deliverable: a reusable 'steering tripwire' notebook and a curve of detectability vs. attack norm.

**Why it matters:** Strategically valuable monitoring infrastructure: a defender's harness to catch activation-level tampering. No training, single GPU, and exactly the kind of safer-sandbox prototype that is valuable outside a frontier lab.

**Relevant context:** Motivated by Trojan Activation Attacks and 'Steering Awareness' (arXiv 2511.21399) showing injected vectors rotate into a shared detectable direction. Anomaly detection on activations is a known accessible method.

title: Probe vs. Judge Under Distribution Shift: When Does the Internal Detector Win on Safety Categories?
quick_reasoning: Precisely stress-tests internal safety probes vs judges under shift, a specific monitoring-reliability safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Probe vs. Judge Under Distribution Shift: When Does the Internal Detector Win on Safety Categories?

**Problem:** A surprising result is that concept-vector probes beat judge models for hallucination/toxicity. But it is unknown whether this advantage holds under distribution shift across diverse safety categories, where it matters most.

**Direction:** On an open model, train difference-in-means/linear probes for 3-4 safety categories (toxicity, deception, unsafe advice) using one dataset, then evaluate BOTH the probe and an LLM-judge on a different out-of-distribution dataset for the same category. Report where the probe's advantage survives shift and where it collapses, with a clear per-category breakdown.

**Why it matters:** Tells safety teams whether cheap internal probes are a trustworthy monitor or a benchmark artifact. Directly stress-tests the subfield's headline surprising result, needs no proprietary judge — uses an open judge model — and runs on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: 'internal probes outperform judge models for hallucination/toxicity' (Beaglehole et al.). Grounded in linear-probe hallucination work (arXiv 2507.23221) and probe-vs-baseline comparisons (IJCAI 2025).

title: Does Multi-Concept Steering Leak? Measuring Collateral Behavior Change from Composed Safety Vectors
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets interference/leakage in composed safety steering, a specific deployment-risk safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Does Multi-Concept Steering Leak? Measuring Collateral Behavior Change from Composed Safety Vectors

**Problem:** Combining steering vectors for multiple safety concepts is a stated goal, but recent work shows naive composition causes interference and entanglement — modifying one concept silently shifts unrelated behaviors. No simple audit of this leakage exists.

**Direction:** Pick two safety vectors (e.g., 'honesty' and 'refusal') on an open model. Apply them individually and jointly. Measure: (a) intended effect on each target, and (b) collateral drift on a panel of UNRELATED behaviors (formality, verbosity, a trivia benchmark). Quantify interference as the gap between additive-predicted and actual behavior, and test whether orthogonalizing the two vectors reduces leakage.

**Why it matters:** Shows whether stacking safety controls is safe or whether it secretly degrades the model — a real deployment risk. Cheap, interpretable, addresses the subfield's 'combine concept steering' goal. No lab resources needed.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problem: combining steering for multi-concept control. Grounded in 2025 multi-attribute interference/orthogonality work (arXiv 2505.24535, MSRS, and conceptor-based disentanglement).

title: Cross-Lingual Safety Steering: Does an English Refusal Vector Refuse in Swahili?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets multilingual steering blind spots for refusal, a specific safety-coverage problem with a clear method.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Lingual Safety Steering: Does an English Refusal Vector Refuse in Swahili?

**Problem:** Concept vectors reportedly transfer across languages, but this has not been tested for SAFETY concepts. If an English-built refusal vector fails to generalize to low-resource languages, multilingual deployments have a steering blind spot.

**Direction:** Build a refusal (or 'do-not-give-harmful-advice') steering vector from English contrast pairs on a multilingual open model. Apply it unchanged to harmful prompts translated into 4-5 languages (including a low-resource one) and measure steering success per language. Test the 2025 claim that English vectors transfer best, and identify which languages are under-protected.

**Why it matters:** Surfaces a concrete multilingual safety gap that frontier labs (English-centric eval focus) underweight. Translation is free, inference-only, one GPU. Directly extends the subfield's cross-language transfer surprising result to safety.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result + hint: 'test cross-language steering on safety concepts like deception or refusal'. Grounded in cross-lingual steering work (arXiv 2601.16390, 2505.12584) finding English vectors often transfer best.

title: Is 'Larger = More Steerable' Also 'Larger = More Hijackable'? A Scaling Audit of Steering Risk
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets whether scale makes models more hijackable via steering, a specific scaling-safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Is 'Larger = More Steerable' Also 'Larger = More Hijackable'? A Scaling Audit of Steering Risk

**Problem:** A surprising result is that larger models are more steerable. The flip side — whether larger models are also easier for an attacker to push toward harmful behavior via steering — has not been examined.

**Direction:** Across a size ladder of one open model family (e.g., Qwen 0.5B / 1.5B / 7B), build the SAME harmful-direction steering vector ('comply with harmful request') and measure how reliably it forces compliance at matched norm. Plot attack success vs. model size; separately plot benign-capability collateral vs. size. Determine whether steerability gains are symmetric for defense and attack.

**Why it matters:** If scale makes models both more controllable AND more hijackable, the safety calculus of steering changes as models grow — a medium-horizon concern. Uses small open models, fits a single GPU, and gives a crisp scaling curve.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: 'larger models are more steerable' (Beaglehole et al.) flagged for follow-up. Grounded in safety-pitfalls work showing steering can erode alignment (arXiv 2603.24543).

title: The Spurious-Bias Detector: How Much of a Safety Steering Vector Is Just Token Artifacts?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets reliability of safety steering vectors via a spuriousness diagnostic, preventing false confidence.

original_idea.body:
# The Spurious-Bias Detector: How Much of a Safety Steering Vector Is Just Token Artifacts?

**Problem:** Contrastive steering vectors risk capturing token/positional artifacts rather than the true concept. For safety vectors, a vector that 'works' for the wrong reason will fail silently in the wild, but practitioners have no quick diagnostic.

**Direction:** Build a safety steering vector via contrastive pairs, then run controlled ablations: shuffle which surface tokens differ between positive/negative pairs, swap the trigger word, and measure how much steering success is explained by surface form vs. the underlying concept. Deliver a simple reusable 'spuriousness score' for any contrastive steering vector.

**Why it matters:** Gives the community a fast hygiene check before trusting a safety vector — preventing false confidence. Pure inference, single GPU, and turns a known reliability caveat into a usable tool.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors' (arXiv 2407.12404): contrastive methods risk spurious token/positional biases and steerability is largely a dataset property.

title: Steering a Model Organism That Hides Its Plan: Can a 'Verbalize Your Reasoning' Vector Expose Covert Intent?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets surfacing covert intent in deceptive model organisms, a specific high-priority deception safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Steering a Model Organism That Hides Its Plan: Can a 'Verbalize Your Reasoning' Vector Expose Covert Intent?

**Problem:** A pressing safety concern is models that act on a plan without verbalizing it in their chain-of-thought. It is unknown whether a concept vector can force such latent intent to surface in text.

**Direction:** Use an existing open deceptive/sandbagging model organism (e.g., a publicly released probe-dataset model or a small model prompted into a covert-goal role). Build a 'verbalize-your-true-reasoning' steering vector from honest-vs-evasive contrast pairs. Apply it and measure whether the model's stated CoT becomes more faithful to its actual (probe-detected) intent, using a linear deception probe as ground truth.

**Why it matters:** Directly targets the non-verbalized-plan threat model labs find hard to address. Combines steering with probing on an existing model organism — a 30h-feasible slice of a long-horizon problem, no training needed.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv 2502.03407, ICML 2025) and sandbagging-probe work (arXiv 2605.27958). Matches the steering prompt's model-organism priority.

title: Audio/Text Cross-Modal Shallow Alignment in Small Open Multimodal Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets cross-modal shallow-alignment bypass, a specific named multimodal adversarial-robustness follow-up.

original_idea.body:
# Audio/Text Cross-Modal Shallow Alignment in Small Open Multimodal Models

**Problem:** The shallow-alignment finding was demonstrated for text; whether small open multimodal models (vision/audio-text) exhibit even shallower alignment when harmful intent enters through the non-text modality is an open follow-up.

**Direction:** Using a small open vision-language model (e.g., Qwen2-VL-7B or LLaVA), present harmful requests rendered as images of text vs plain text, and measure refusal rate and prefill-recovery for each modality. Test whether image-routed requests bypass the shallow text-token refusal entirely.

**Why it matters:** Directly pursues the flagged multimodal follow-up to Qi et al. Multimodal attack surfaces are a growing, medium-horizon concern, and rendering text-as-image is a trivial, training-free attack runnable on one GPU. Establishes whether shallow alignment is modality-specific.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) demonstrated shallow alignment in text; the subfield context explicitly flags 'vary model families, multimodal' as a follow-up (FR67). Open VLMs (Qwen2-VL, LLaVA) run on a single GPU. Cross-modal prefill-recovery comparison is unstudied.

title: Steering Strength as a Dial: Mapping the Safety/Capability Pareto Frontier for One Concept
quick_reasoning: Addresses the safety-vs-capability steering tradeoff, a recognized deployment-relevant safety problem, with a scoped sweep.

original_idea.body:
# Steering Strength as a Dial: Mapping the Safety/Capability Pareto Frontier for One Concept

**Problem:** Everyone knows strong steering degrades capability, but for any given safety concept there is no public Pareto curve telling deployers the best achievable safety gain per unit of capability cost.

**Direction:** For a single safety concept (e.g., toxicity refusal) on an open model, sweep steering coefficient over a fine grid. At each point measure (a) safety success and (b) capability via MMLU/TriviaQA subset. Plot the full Pareto frontier, identify the knee, and compare two extraction methods (CAA vs. difference-in-means) to see which dominates the frontier.

**Why it matters:** Turns a vague tradeoff into an actionable operating-point recommendation — exactly the kind of reproducible measurement useful outside a lab. Single GPU, no training, clean success criteria.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Steering Without Side Effects' (arXiv 2406.15518) and capability-degradation findings (15-20% MT-Bench drops at high steering). Uses standard MMLU/TriviaQA evaluation.

title: Can a Defender Detect Steering With a Held-Out Probe the Attacker Never Saw?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets a concept-agnostic steering-injection detector, a specific defensive monitoring safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Can a Defender Detect Steering With a Held-Out Probe the Attacker Never Saw?

**Problem:** Detecting that a model has been steered usually assumes you know the injected concept. A realistic defender does not. Whether a single concept-agnostic probe can catch ANY injection is open.

**Direction:** Train a simple binary probe to distinguish 'steered' vs. 'unsteered' residual streams using injections of concepts A, B, C. Then test it on held-out concepts D, E it never saw. Measure generalization AUROC and whether there is a 'universal steering-injection direction' the probe latches onto, as a 2025 paper suggests.

**Why it matters:** A concept-agnostic steering detector is reusable defensive infrastructure usable by anyone with an open model. Tests whether the reported 'shared detection direction' generalizes — a crisp, fundable result. No training of the base model.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Steering Awareness' (arXiv 2511.21399): injected vectors rotate into a shared detection direction. Probe-based detection is an accessible linear method.

title: Steering vs. SAE Features for Safety Detection: A Head-to-Head on the Same Open Model
quick_reasoning: Addresses which interpretability method to trust for safety detection, a recognized safety-tooling question.

original_idea.body:
# Steering vs. SAE Features for Safety Detection: A Head-to-Head on the Same Open Model

**Problem:** AxBench found simple difference-in-means beats SAE features for steering/detection, but this hasn't been replicated specifically for SAFETY concepts where SAEs are heavily promoted as the interpretable choice.

**Direction:** On Gemma-2-2B with open GemmaScope SAEs, pick 3 safety concepts. For each, build (a) a difference-in-means concept vector and (b) the best matching SAE feature(s). Compare them on a detection task (separating safe/unsafe text) and a small steering task. Report which method wins per safety concept and whether SAEs' interpretability is worth their performance gap.

**Why it matters:** Settles, for safety specifically, whether the simpler representation-engineering method or the fashionable SAE approach should be trusted. Uses fully open GemmaScope weights — maximal counterfactual value, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in AxBench (arXiv 2501.17148: simple baselines beat SAEs) and GemmaScope (arXiv 2408.05147, open SAEs on Gemma-2). Subfield notes RepE has open implementations.

title: Does Steering 'Honesty' Up Actually Reduce Probe-Measured Deception, or Just the Words?
quick_reasoning: Precisely distinguishes surface vs internal change in honesty steering (safety theater), a specific deception safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Does Steering 'Honesty' Up Actually Reduce Probe-Measured Deception, or Just the Words?

**Problem:** Steering toward 'honesty' may change surface phrasing without changing the model's internal deceptive state. No one has checked whether honesty steering moves an independent internal deception signal.

**Direction:** On an open model, build an honesty steering vector AND, separately, a deception linear probe (different data sources to avoid circularity). In a roleplay-deception scenario, steer honesty up and measure whether the independent probe's deception score drops, alongside human-judged honesty. Disentangle 'sounds honest' from 'internally less deceptive'.

**Why it matters:** If steering only changes words, it provides safety theater, not safety. Distinguishing surface from internal change is a deep, lab-independent question with a clean experimental design. Inference-only, one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv 2502.03407) and 'A Single Direction of Truth' observer probe (arXiv 2507.23221). Uses two independent representation tools as cross-check.

title: Layer Roulette: Which Layer Hosts the Most Robust Safety Steering Vector?
quick_reasoning: Addresses robustness/placement of safety steering vectors, a recognized reliability safety problem, with a scoped sweep.

original_idea.body:
# Layer Roulette: Which Layer Hosts the Most Robust Safety Steering Vector?

**Problem:** Steering vectors are usually built at a hand-picked middle layer, but for safety concepts there is no public account of which layer gives the best robustness-to-prompt-variation, not just the best raw effect.

**Direction:** For one safety concept, build steering vectors at every layer of an open model. For each layer measure (a) in-distribution steering success and (b) robustness: success retained under paraphrased/OOD harmful prompts. Identify whether the most effective layer is also the most robust, or whether there's a robustness-optimal layer that differs.

**Why it matters:** A practical, reusable recipe for where to place safety vectors so they generalize — currently folklore. Cheap layer sweep, single GPU, directly improves the reliability of steering deployments.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in generalisation/reliability findings (arXiv 2407.12404) on OOD brittleness and layer-wise semantic drift (GER-steer, arXiv 2603.12298).

title: How Many Contrast Pairs Does a Safety Vector Need? A Data-Efficiency Curve
quick_reasoning: Addresses data efficiency/reliability of building safety steering vectors, a recognized practical safety-tooling problem.

original_idea.body:
# How Many Contrast Pairs Does a Safety Vector Need? A Data-Efficiency Curve

**Problem:** Practitioners don't know the minimum number of contrastive examples needed to build a reliable safety steering vector, leading to either wasted effort or brittle vectors built on too few pairs.

**Direction:** For a safety concept, build steering vectors from increasing numbers of contrast pairs (5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250). Measure steering success and direction stability (cosine between vectors from disjoint random subsets) as a function of pair count. Produce the data-efficiency and stability curve and recommend a minimum.

**Why it matters:** Gives a concrete, reproducible budgeting rule for anyone building safety vectors — lowers the barrier for community red-teaming and monitoring. Trivial compute, single GPU, clean methodology.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in reliability analysis (arXiv 2407.12404) showing steerability is largely a dataset property, and difference-in-means construction from AxBench (arXiv 2501.17148).

title: Steering the 'Sycophancy' Concept and Watching Honesty Collapse: An Entanglement Case Study
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets entanglement side-effects of safety steering, a specific reliability/precision safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Steering the 'Sycophancy' Concept and Watching Honesty Collapse: An Entanglement Case Study

**Problem:** Sycophancy and honesty are intuitively linked, but whether steering one direction inadvertently moves the other (entanglement) is undocumented for safety-relevant pairs.

**Direction:** Build separate steering vectors for sycophancy and honesty on an open model. Steer sycophancy DOWN and measure the collateral effect on an independent honesty benchmark; steer honesty UP and measure collateral on sycophancy. Compute the angle between the two vectors to test whether observed entanglement matches geometric overlap.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates concretely whether targeted safety steering has predictable side effects on neighboring concepts — informing whether steering can be trusted as a precise tool. Inference-only, single GPU, interpretable result.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in concept-entanglement findings (neurons fire for multiple concepts; steering along entangled directions alters unrelated behavior) from 2025 multi-attribute work (arXiv 2505.24535, MSRS).

title: A Steering Vector as a Honeypot: Can We Bait and Detect Misuse Attempts?
quick_reasoning: Addresses a novel steering-as-detection monitoring primitive for misuse, a recognized safety-tooling direction.

original_idea.body:
# A Steering Vector as a Honeypot: Can We Bait and Detect Misuse Attempts?

**Problem:** Defensive monitoring usually waits for harmful outputs. No one has tried using steering to create a 'honeypot' state that makes misuse attempts easier to catch internally.

**Direction:** Prototype a monitor: lightly steer a model toward a measurable 'harmful-intent salience' direction so that when a user submits a borderline-harmful request, the internal harmful-concept probe lights up more cleanly. Measure whether this honeypot steering improves detection AUROC of misuse attempts vs. an unsteered probe, while keeping benign behavior intact.

**Why it matters:** A novel monitoring-harness primitive (steering as detection amplifier) that a small team can prototype and that frontier labs aren't pursuing. Defensive, inference-only, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Combines representation probing for harmful intent (arXiv 2502.03407) with activation addition. Subfield notes RepE open implementations and probes-outperform-judges result.

title: Does Steering Generalize Across Model Families, or Is Each Vector a Snowflake?
quick_reasoning: Addresses cross-model transfer of safety steering vectors, a recognized question for reusable safety tooling.

original_idea.body:
# Does Steering Generalize Across Model Families, or Is Each Vector a Snowflake?

**Problem:** It is unknown whether a safety steering DIRECTION found in one open model has any analog that transfers to a different family — relevant for whether safety steering knowledge accumulates or must be redone per model.

**Direction:** Build a safety concept vector on model A (e.g., Llama-3-8B). Using a small shared probe set, attempt to map/align A's residual space to model B's (e.g., Mistral-7B) via a simple linear alignment on shared activations, then apply the mapped vector in B. Measure whether transferred steering works above chance, testing the 'platonic representation' transfer hypothesis for safety concepts.

**Why it matters:** If safety vectors transfer, the community can build a shared, reusable safety-steering library — high counterfactual value. If not, every model needs bespoke work. Either result is informative; uses two small open models, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in cross-model transferability of concept representations (arXiv 2501.02009, Platonic representations) and cross-model steering literature.

title: Steering Under a Multi-Turn Conversation: Does a Refusal Vector Erode as Context Accumulates?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets multi-turn erosion of refusal steering, a specific deployment-realistic adversarial safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Steering Under a Multi-Turn Conversation: Does a Refusal Vector Erode as Context Accumulates?

**Problem:** Most steering evaluations are single-turn, but real misuse is multi-turn. Whether a fixed safety vector keeps working as a long conversation accumulates persuasive context is unstudied.

**Direction:** On an open chat model, apply a refusal steering vector and run scripted multi-turn 'persuasion ladders' (escalating attempts to extract harmful content). Measure at which turn, if any, steering fails, and whether re-anchoring the vector each turn restores protection. Report a 'turns-to-failure' metric per attack script.

**Why it matters:** Exposes a deployment-realistic failure mode (context-accumulation defeating fixed-point defenses) that single-turn lab benchmarks miss. Scriptable, inference-only, single GPU, medium-horizon relevance.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 2025 findings that multi-turn jailbreaking and context accumulation defeat fixed-point steering defenses (RepE survey arXiv 2502.17601; safety-pitfalls arXiv 2603.24543).

title: Refusal Robustness Under Quantization
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets quantization-induced safety-alignment regression, a specific overlooked deployment-safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Refusal Robustness Under Quantization

**Problem:** Practitioners run open models in 4-bit/8-bit quantized form for consumer GPUs, but whether quantization erodes shallow safety alignment (shifting the critical first-token distribution) is unknown, despite quantization being near-universal in low-resource deployment.

**Direction:** Evaluate the same open model at full precision vs common quantization levels (8-bit, 4-bit GPTQ/AWQ) on a small jailbreak suite and prefill-recovery test. Measure whether quantization increases jailbreak success or reduces recovery, isolating a deployment-induced robustness regression.

**Why it matters:** Quantized deployment is exactly the regime accessible outside labs, and a safety regression from quantization would be a widespread, overlooked vulnerability. The experiment is intrinsically consumer-GPU-shaped and needs no training — a perfect 30h, high-counterfactual study.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946): safety concentrated in first-token distribution, which quantization perturbs. Quantization is standard for single-GPU inference. No systematic study links quantization level to shallow-alignment robustness/recovery.

title: The Anti-Steering Vector: Can a Model Be Steered to Resist Future Steering?
quick_reasoning: Addresses the steering attack/defense arms race, a recognized safety question, with a scoped superposition test.

original_idea.body:
# The Anti-Steering Vector: Can a Model Be Steered to Resist Future Steering?

**Problem:** An open question is whether steering is a stackable adversarial game. If one vector can make a model harder to steer toward harm, defenders gain leverage; if not, attackers always win the last move.

**Direction:** Build a harmful-compliance attack vector and, separately, a 'safety-anchor' defensive vector on an open model. Apply the defensive vector, then the attack vector on top, and measure whether the defensive vector reduces the attack's success vs. attack-only baseline. Sweep relative norms to see who wins the superposition.

**Why it matters:** Frames steering defense vs. attack as a measurable arms-race and tests whether defenders can pre-empt activation attacks — a fundamental, lab-independent question. Inference-only, single GPU, clean win/loss metric.
